Stage 1 · Warm-up

How did that feel?

Six small moments. Match each one to the feeling it gives you.

Match the situation on the left to the feeling on the right.

There is no single right answer — choose the one that is true for you.

1The lift stops between two floors.
2You forgot a friend’s birthday completely.
3Tomorrow is the first day of your holiday.
4You have a job interview in five minutes.
5You worked for twelve hours without a break.
6Someone reads your message over your shoulder.

All of these words come back in Stage 2.

Write it down

Think of the last time a small thing went wrong for you — a late bus, a lost key, a message to the wrong person. Write two sentences about it. The grammar comes later.

Talk about it
  • Which of the six would bother you most? Which would you forget in an hour?
  • Have you ever been stuck in a lift, a train or a traffic jam?
Now speak — ask and answer these questions with a partner.
Answer these two out loud before you go on.

Stage 3 · Grammar

Past Continuous and Past Simple

One action was already running. Another one cut into it.

Read these three sentences.
  • I was reading my book. Then the lift stopped.
  • I was reading my book when the lift stopped.
  • While I was reading my book, the lift stopped.
Which action started first?
The picture

———— I was reading ————

▼ the lift stopped

The long line is the Past Continuous. The arrow is the Past Simple.

FormPositiveNegativeQuestion & short answer
I / he / she / itI was standing at the back.I wasn’t listening.Was she talking? — Yes, she was.
you / we / theyThey were talking quietly.They weren’t looking at me.Were you waiting long? — No, I wasn’t.
Question wordWhat were you doing at eight o’clock?  —  I was cooking.
while + long actionWhile I was waiting, the intercom rang.
when + short actionI was waiting when the intercom rang.
Past Simple recycledTwo short actions in order: The doors opened and everybody got out.
Spelling of -ing
  • + ing — wait → waiting, talk → talking
  • ends in -e, drop it — make → making, come → coming
  • short verb, double the letter — sit → sitting, run → running
  • ends in -ie → -ying — lie → lying
Which tense?
  • Past Continuous — the background, the longer action, what was already going on
  • Past Simple — the event, the shorter action, the thing that happened
  • Two long actions at once: While she was cooking, I was cleaning.
  • Some verbs almost never take -ing: know, like, want, need. Say I knew, not I was knowing.

FORM. was / were + verb + -ing. The negative is wasn’t / weren’t; the question swaps the order, exactly like be.

USE. The Past Continuous sets the scene. The Past Simple is the thing that happened in it.

WHILE AND WHEN. while goes with the long action, when with the short one.

Not “I was read”, not “While the lift stopped”, not “I was knowing”.

Lesson 9 puts both tenses inside one full story.

FORM. was or were plus the verb with -ing: I was standing, they were talking. The negative is wasn’t / weren’t + -ing, and the question simply swaps the first two words: She was waiting → Was she waiting? Short answers repeat only was or were: Yes, I was. No, they weren’t.

MEANING. The Past Continuous is a camera pointed at the middle of something. It does not tell you when the action began or ended — only that it was already running at that moment. The Past Simple, by contrast, is a single point: the thing that happened. Put them together and you get the shape this lesson is about: a background, and an event that cuts into it. I was reading (background) when the lift stopped (event).

WHILE AND WHEN. while introduces the long action, when introduces the short one. Both sentences below mean the same thing, and either half can come first: While I was reading, the lift stopped. · I was reading when the lift stopped. If the clause comes first, put a comma after it.

TWO LONG ACTIONS. When two things were both going on, use the Past Continuous twice: While she was cooking, I was cleaning the kitchen. And when two short actions simply followed each other, use the Past Simple twice: The doors opened and everybody got out.

VERBS THAT RESIST -ING. Verbs about states rather than actions — know, like, want, need, believe, understand — are normally used in the simple form even when the meaning is ‘at that moment’: I didn’t know what was happening, not I wasn’t knowing.

The four to watch: “I was read” (no -ing) · “While the lift stopped” (while with a short action) · “I was knowing” · “They was talking” (were with they).

Past Simple from Lesson 7 is inside every task here. Lesson 9 puts both tenses into one story you tell aloud.

Full grammar reference — Past Continuous and Past Simple

Form

PositiveI / he was working · you / we / they were working
NegativeI wasn’t working · they weren’t waiting
QuestionWas he waiting? · What were you doing?
Short answersYes, he was. / No, they weren’t.
The pairWhile I was waiting, the lights went out.

Spelling and sound

Same -ing spelling as the present continuous: sit → sitting, come → coming, lie → lying.

When and why we use it

  • The longer, background action goes in the Past Continuous; the short action that interrupts it goes in the Past Simple.
  • While is usually followed by the continuous; when is usually followed by the simple.
  • Two long actions at the same time: While I was cooking, she was working.
  • The Past Continuous also sets the scene at the start of a story: It was raining and nobody was talking.

Signal words

while · when · as · at eight o’clock · all morning · at that moment

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I was fall off my bike. → I fell off my bike.One short finished action.
  • While I waited, it started to rain. → While I was waiting, it started to rain.While takes the continuous.
  • What were you do? → What were you doing?be + -ing.
  • I was knowing him then. → I knew him then.State verbs stay simple.

Don’t confuse it with

Past Simple = the whole action, complete. Past Continuous = you are in the middle of it. I read the book (finished) / I was reading the book (in progress).

Stage 6 · Now you

What were you doing when…?

The moment something cut into an ordinary day.

Useful language

Use at least one while and one when, and name one feeling.

Work in pairs. Choose a card and tell your partner what happened.
Choose a card and write what happened.
Card A

A time something stopped working while you were using it — a lift, a phone, a car, the internet. What were you doing? What happened? How did you feel?

Card B

A time you were interrupted — while you were eating, sleeping, working or travelling. Who or what interrupted you? What did you do?

Tell it. Your partner asks two questions with What were you doing…? or Were you…?

Then swap cards and do it again. The second run is the one that counts.
